meta.title: Designing Web APIs
meta.author: Brenda Jin, Saurabh Sahni, and Amir Shevat

sentences: APIs play a vital role in modern software development by allowing programs to interface with one another, **enabling interoperability** just like **LEGO bricks** connect.
This book is about building **developer-friendly APIs** from scratch.
Originally, APIs were developed to solve problems more efficiently without individual programmers having to reinvent the wheel, such as embedding Google Maps or using Facebook Login functionalities.
They provide **value quickly** and allow startups to **differentiate** their products by tapping into established services.
Developers can innovate and build products on platforms like **Slack** using these integrations.
Designing a successful API involves carefully understanding your **developer's needs** and aligning with your company's core business strategy, much like GitHub does.

parts.title: APIs as Core Products and Key Design Considerations

sentences: APIs are crucial in the modern tech landscape, serving as essential components for developers.
**Stripe** and **Twilio** exemplify companies where the API itself is the core product.

For an API to be considered great, it must effectively solve problems, provide clarity in its purpose, offer flexibility, complete its intended task comprehensively, be easy to iterate on, and have excellent documentation.
However, a good API also needs to be built with a strategy to withstand changes over time.
**REST, RPC, and GraphQL** are popular paradigms for defining API interfaces.

Each has its **strengths and weaknesses**, like REST's resource-based approach and GraphQL's flexible querying options, which can save developers time by preventing multiple round trips and reduce payload sizes.

parts.title: Understanding API Security: Importance and Practices

paragraphs.heading: Understanding API Security: Importance and Practices
sentences: Security is **critical** for any web **application**, and even more so for **APIs**.
There are essential tasks that engineers must undertake to ensure security, including:

- **Input Validation** - Use of **Secure Sockets Layer (SSL)** - **Content Type Validation** - Maintaining **audit logs** - Protection against **Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** and **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)**
Beyond these practices, APIs exposed to **external developers** demand additional **security measures**.
This segment zeroes in on these **specialized** strategies for securing **APIs** in real-world contexts.

paragraphs.heading: Delving into Authentication and Authorization
sentences: Two fundamental aspects of API **security** are:
**Authentication** – Verifying **identity** by matching usernames and **passwords**.
This function ensures that requests are **genuine**.
**Authorization** – Determining **permissions** for accessing resources, allowing specific actions based on user roles (e.g., viewing but not editing pages unless you are an **admin**).
While many APIs initially opted for **Basic Authentication**, where users shared their **credentials** directly, it has significant drawbacks, such as:
- **Credential Exposure** – Apps might store passwords in text, risking data breach.
- Limited **Access Control** – Users couldn't revoke app access selectively.
- **Unrestricted Access** – Apps gained more access than necessary.
When designing an **API**, focus on real-world use cases and create clear **key user stories** to guide your work.
APIs should provide a great **developer experience**—being intuitive, fast, and easy to start using.
Ensure **consistency** in naming and responses to help developers predict usage without extensive documentation.
Offer clear, actionable **error messages** and build tools to aid troubleshooting, like **interactive documentation** and **SDKs**.
Design APIs to be **extensible** and maintain **backward compatibility**; consider versioning if you anticipate changes.

parts.title: Scaling APIs: Throughput and Resource Management Strategies

sentences: Addressing API scaling challenges involves a step-by-step process.

Key methods include optimizing resource usage (via disk, network, CPU, and memory), adding computing resources (such as vertical and horizontal scaling), creating database indexes, and implementing caching (both standard and edge caching).
The Slack case study illustrates how rebuilding API architecture to reduce HTTP requests through a service called Flannel resulted in substantial performance improvement.
The emphasis on improving API design and optimizing requests is essential for handling increased usage effectively and ensuring high performance.
To **scale APIs** effectively, Slack and other companies have addressed various bottlenecks by evolving their API **design**.
This includes **rate-limiting**, **pagination**, and adding methods that perform **operations asynchronously**.
For instance, Slack transitioned from a Real-Time Messaging API to an **Events API** to handle data more efficiently using Webhooks, which reduced server load and made development easier.
They also introduced **bulk endpoints** to perform actions on multiple items, increasing efficiency by requiring fewer API calls.

parts.title: Managing Rate Limits and Best Practices for APIs

sentences: **Rate Limit Indicators**: APIs have headers like **X-RateLimit-Limit** (max requests), **X-RateLimit-Remaining** (requests left), and **X-RateLimit-Reset** (reset time in UTC seconds) to inform developers about capacity.
**Importance of Rate Limits**: Proper rate-limit documentation is crucial for developers to plan their API usage and avoid disruptions.
**Best Practices** include starting with low thresholds, using exponential back-offs, and accommodating infrastructure to support necessary quotas.
Examples from GitHub and Slack illustrate design considerations and adjustments to ensure developer satisfaction and application stability.

parts.title: Building and Nurturing a Developer Ecosystem

sentences: **Developers** are essential to maximizing the potential of an API.
They can extend your product's value, become your clients, or help grow your platform.
Understanding different **developer segments**, such as **hobbyists**, **professional developers**, and **business-focused users**, is crucial.
Each group has different needs, levels of proficiency, and motivations for using your API.

Creating a **developer strategy** involves segmenting your audience, understanding their identities and proficiencies, and crafting a **value proposition** that highlights why developers should use your API.
Building a **funnel** helps track the journey from awareness to success, enabling clear **tactics** to move developers through these stages.
Evaluating your current state and setting realistic short-term and long-term goals is also important for growing your ecosystem.
Before starting your plan, it's crucial to link developer actions to **measurements** to ensure progress and impact.
Think about the **metric** you aim to affect with each activity.
Evaluate if your targets are achieved post-activity.
For instance, after hosting an event, measure how many developers run a **hands-on lab** and track if they become active developers.
The effect of a **design sprint** can be assessed by checking if partners implement the recommendations to enhance API use.
Track every activity to see if it has moved the needle in the right direction.
For effective measurement, identify **KPIs** and link them to activities.
**Examples** include: for a **Developer awareness** KPI, measure **Website entry** before and after speaking at an event to track new developer engagement.
Similarly, for **Proficiency** KPIs, track **Tokens created** after conducting technical workshops to measure efficacy.
Creativity is encouraged in activities to influence KPIs, but staying consistent helps in tracking **long-term** progress.
Maintaining a consistent and thought-out API design is important when launching new features.
**Slack's launch process** is highlighted to demonstrate a comprehensive **beta program**, ensuring that **top developers** adopt new features and provide feedback.
This process involves six stages: ideation, recruitment, onboarding, joint building, launch preparation, and launch day, all aimed at fostering a strong **developer ecosystem**.
It is advised to be very hands-on with **beta developers** to ensure the program's success.
